chapterNote: The exiles' psalm, and the hardest in the Psalter to sing to the end. By the rivers of Babylon — the irrigation canals of the Euphrates — the deported sat and wept, remembering Zion, and hung their lyres on the poplars because their captors demanded entertainment: sing us one of the songs of Zion. The answer is the psalm's first great line: how could we sing the LORD's song on foreign soil? Then the vow that has bound Jews to Jerusalem for some twenty-six centuries: if I forget you, O Jerusalem, may my right hand forget its skill; let my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth if I do not lift Jerusalem above the peak of my joy. And then the end, which the church has not known what to do with: remember Edom, who cheered the demolition. And you, daughter of Babylon, marked for devastation: happy the one who repays you what you did to us, happy the one who seizes your little ones and dashes them against the rock. It is not a command to the church; it is a wound handed to God in prayer — and a prayer that asks for nothing God had not already announced against Babylon through Isaiah and Jeremiah (Isaiah 13:16; Jeremiah 51:24) — and it asks for Babylon only what the prophets had already foretold for her (Isaiah 13:16) — the siege atrocity Jerusalem's own children had just suffered (Lamentations 2:11-12; 4:4, 10). The psalm does not sanitize what exile feels like, and it does not tell the exiles to lie about it to God. Augustine read the infants as sins dashed on Christ the Rock while they are still small; the church has kept the psalm because grief this honest belongs in the prayer book.

1.text: Beside the rivers of Babylon — there we sat, and there we wept, as we remembered Zion.
1.amp: By the rivers [nahar] of Babylon [Babel], there we sat down [yashab], yea, we wept [bakah], when we remembered [zakar] Zion [Tsiyyon].
1.notes: al naharot Babel (H5104, H894): the rivers of Babylon — the Euphrates and the great irrigation canals, the Chebar of Ezekiel 1:1 — sham yashabnu gam-bakhinu (H3427, H1058): there we sat, yes, we wept — be-zokhrenu et-Tsiyyon (H2142, H6726): when we remembered Zion. The most famous opening in the Psalter after the twenty-third, and the saddest.

2.text: On the poplars in the midst of it we hung up our lyres.
2.amp: We hanged [talah] our harps [kinnor — lyres] upon the willows [arab — poplars] in the midst [tavek] thereof.
2.notes: al-arabim be-tokhah talinu kinnorotenu (H6155, H8432, H8518, H3658): the arabim — most likely the Euphrates poplar (the KJV's 'willows'), the tree that lines the canals — with the kinnorot, David's lyres, hung on them like something put away. Musicians who will not play; the instruments of the temple choir retired to a tree.

3.text: For there our captors demanded songs of us, and our tormentors, mirth: 'Sing us one of the songs of Zion!'
3.amp: For there they that carried us away captive [shabah] required [shaal — asked, demanded] of us a song ['the words of a song', dabar shir, the KJV margin]; and they that wasted ['laid us on heaps', tolal — tormentors, the KJV margin] us required of us mirth [simchah], saying, Sing [shir] us one of the songs [shir] of Zion [Tsiyyon].
3.notes: ki sham sheelunu shobenu dibre-shir (H7592, H7617, H1697, H7892): our captors asked for song-words — ve-tolalenu simchah (H8437, H8057): our tormentors, for merriment — shiru lanu mi-shir Tsiyyon (H7891, H6726): sing us some Zion-song. The temple's music as a conquered people's party trick; the cruelty is the request itself.

4.text: How could we sing the LORD's song on foreign soil?
4.amp: How shall we sing [shir] the LORD'S [YHWH] song [shir] in a strange ['land of a stranger', nekar, the KJV margin] land [adamah — ground, soil]?
4.notes: ekh nashir et-shir-YHWH al admat nekar (H7891, H7892, H3068, H127, H5236): how sing the LORD's song on the SOIL of a stranger — adamah, the ground itself, foreign. Not 'we refuse' but 'how could we': the songs belonged to a place and a Presence; sung as cabaret in Babylon they would have been a lie.

5.text: If I ever forget you, O Jerusalem, may my right hand forget its skill.
5.amp: If I forget [shakach] you, O Jerusalem [Yerushalaim], let my right hand [yamin] forget [shakach] her cunning.
5.notes: im-eshkachekh Yerushalaim tishkach yemini (H7911, H3389, H3225): if I forget you, let my right hand forget — the Hebrew stops there; 'her cunning' is supplied: let the hand that plays the lyre forget how. The exile binds his own body to the city's memory; at many Jewish weddings the groom still recites this verse before the glass is broken in memory of the Temple.

6.text: May my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth if I fail to remember you, if I do not lift Jerusalem above the peak of my joy.
6.amp: If I do not remember [zakar] you, let my tongue [lashon] cleave [dabaq] to the roof of my mouth [chek — palate]; if I prefer [alah — raise, set above] not Jerusalem [Yerushalaim] above my chief ['the head of my joy', rosh, the KJV margin] joy [simchah].
6.notes: tidbaq-leshoni le-chikki im-lo ezkerekhi (H1692, H3956, H2441, H2142): the tongue that would not sing for Babylon offers itself as the forfeit if it ever forgets Zion. Then im-lo aaleh et-Yerushalaim al rosh simchati (H5927, H3389, H7218, H8057): if I do not RAISE Jerusalem above the HEAD of my joy, the margin's literal. The hand and the tongue, the two organs of a musician, both pledged.

7.text: Remember, O LORD, against the sons of Edom the day of Jerusalem — how they said, 'Strip it, strip it, down to its foundation!'
7.amp: Remember [zakar], O LORD [YHWH], the children [ben] of Edom [Edom] in the day [yom] of Jerusalem [Yerushalaim]; who said [amar], Rase ['Make bare', arah — strip naked, the KJV margin] it, rase it, even to the foundation [yesod] thereof.
7.notes: zekhor YHWH li-bne Edom et yom Yerushalaim (H2142, H3068, H1121, H123, H3117, H3389): REMEMBER, LORD — the same zakar the exiles used for Zion — against Edom, Esau's people, who cheered the Babylonians on in 586 (cf. Obadiah 10-14; Lamentations 4:21). Then ha-omerim aru aru ad ha-yesod bah (H559, H6168, H3247): 'strip it, strip it, to the foundation' — arah, the naked-verb of Psalm 141:8. The brother-nation's jeer at the demolition.

8.text: O daughter of Babylon, you who are marked for devastation — happy the one who repays you with the very treatment you dealt out to us!
8.amp: O daughter [bath] of Babylon [Babel], who art to be destroyed ['wasted', shadad — devastated, the KJV margin]; happy [esher] shall he be, that rewards ['recompenseth unto thee thy deed which thou didst to us', shalam, the KJV margin] you as you have served [gamal] us.
8.notes: bat-Babel ha-shedudah (H1323, H894, H7703): daughter of Babylon, the devastated one — the devastated one — a passive participle spoken ahead of the event, 'doomed to devastation' (cf. Isaiah 13:19; Jeremiah 51:8) — ashre she-yeshallem-lakh et-gemulekh she-gamalt lanu (H835, H7999, H1576, H1580): happy the one who pays you back your OWN dealing, the margin's literal: exactly what you did to us. The lex talionis in a prayer, handed to God rather than picked up.

9.text: Happy the one who seizes your little ones and dashes them against the rock.
9.amp: Happy [esher] shall he be, that takes [achaz — seizes] and dashes [naphats] your little ones [olal — infants] against the stones ['the rock', sela, the KJV margin].
9.notes: ashre she-yochez ve-nippets et-olalayikh el-ha-sela (H835, H270, H5310, H5768, H5553): happy the one who seizes and dashes your little ones against the rock — the line the church has never been able to sing comfortably, and should not. It names the standard atrocity of ancient siege warfare (cf. 2 Kings 8:12; Hosea 13:16; Nahum 3:10), the fate Lamentations lets us glimpse for Jerusalem's own children (Lamentations 2:11-12; 4:4, 10), and the very thing Isaiah 13:16 foretells for Babylon — an eyewitness's wound, given to God as a prayer rather than acted on, and asking nothing God had not already announced — an eyewitness's wound, given to God as a prayer rather than acted on. Augustine read the olalim, the little ones, as sins dashed on Christ the Rock while still small; the plainer reading is that the psalm refuses to lie to God about what exile felt like, and leaves the repaying to Him (cf. Romans 12:19).
